subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: writing a short usage policy [Action]
passage: On Thursday afternoon in a co-working space in Nairobi, Omar opened a blank page titled 'How we use AI tools' and asked Jin to write it with him. First came the tools the company had licensed. Second, data: no customer records, no keys, no unreleased plans. Third was a rule they argued over for ten minutes and kept: a person reads every AI-written change before it goes into the main code. They held it to one page and printed it, and Omar added a line asking people to say when AI had helped. On Monday, Jin slipped the page into the new-joiner pack. The next hire, a graduate called Wanjiru, read it over coffee and asked two questions that made them add a sentence.

qa.q: Which rule did Omar and Jin argue over for ten minutes and keep?
qa.a: They kept the rule that a person reads every AI-written change before it goes into the main code.

qa.q: What does Omar want from the extra line about saying when AI helped?
qa.a: Omar is cautious about AI-written changes and wants openness, so reviewers know which changes need a closer look.

qa.q: What could the team do to keep the policy alive?
qa.a: They could review the page every few months, since tools and habits change and a fixed page gets out of date.

qa.q: How might Wanjiru see the page in the first days?
qa.a: Wanjiru probably finds it helpful and short enough to read, since two questions led to one added sentence.

grounding: Shows a team writing a one-page guideline on approved tools, data handling and human review of AI-written changes, then sharing it with new joiners.
